ety.text: From Middle English rode, rade (“ride, journey”), from Old English rād (“riding, hostile incursion”), from Proto-West Germanic *raidu, from Proto-Germanic *raidō (“a ride”), from Proto-Indo-European *reydʰ- (“to ride”). Doublet of raid, acquired from Scots. Cognates include West Frisian reed (paved trail/road, driveway).

senses.d: A way used for travelling between places, originally one wide enough to allow foot passengers and horses to travel, now (US) usually one surfaced with asphalt or concrete and designed to accommodate many vehicles travelling in both directions. ex: In the lightness of my heart I sang catches of songs as my horse gayly bore me along the well-remembered road.
And the road doesn't end / It's a long, long road and we follow it again and again / And the road don't pretend

ety.text: From Middle English roren, raren, from Old English rārian (“to roar; wail; lament”), from Proto-West Germanic *rairōn, from Proto-Germanic *rairōną (“to bellow; roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *rey- (“to shout; bellow; yell; bark”), perhaps of imitative origin. Cognate with Saterland Frisian roorje (“to roar”), German röhren (“to roar”).

senses.d: To make a loud, deep cry, especially from pain, anger, or other strong emotion.
ex: Sole on the barren ſands the ſuff'ring chief / Roar'd out for anguiſh, and indulg'd his grief.

Hearing the rout,
Dame Gill came out,
With a horse whip from the door,
She laid it on Jack,
And poor Jill's back,
Until they both did roar.

senses.d: To laugh in a particularly loud manner.
ex: The audience roared at his jokes.

senses.d: Of animals (especially a lion), to make a loud deep noise.
ex: The lioness roared to scare off the hyenas.

senses.d: Generally, of inanimate objects etc., to make a loud resounding noise.
ex: The brazen throat of war had ceased to roar.
How oft I crossed where carts and coaches roar.

senses.d: To proceed vigorously.
To cry aloud; to proclaim loudly.
ex: This last action will roar thy infamy.

senses.d: To be boisterous; to be disorderly.
ex: It was a mad, roaring time, full of extravagance.

senses.d: To make a loud noise in breathing, as horses do when they have a certain disease.

ety.text: From Middle English rosten, a borrowing from Old French rostir (“to roast, to torture with fire”), from Frankish *rōstijan (“to roast, broil”), from Proto-Germanic *raustijaną (“to roast”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hrews- (“to crackle; roast”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian rosterje (“to roast”), Dutch roosten, roosteren (“to roast”), German rösten (“to roast”). Displaced native Middle English breden, bræden (“to roast”), from Old English brǣdan, related to German braten (“to roast, grill”). The noun is from Middle English roste, from Old French rost, roste, from the verb.

senses.d: To cook food by heating in an oven or over a fire without covering, resulting in a crisp, possibly even slightly charred appearance.
ex: to roast meat on a spit

senses.d: To cook by surrounding with hot embers, ashes, sand, etc.
ex: to roast a potato in ashes
In eggs boiled and roasted […]there is scarce difference to be discerned.

senses.d: To process by drying through exposure to sun or artificial heat.
ex: Coffee beans need roasting before use.
to roast chestnuts or peanuts

senses.d: To heat to excess; to heat violently; to burn.
ex: roasted in wrath and fire

senses.d: To admonish someone vigorously.
ex: I'm late home for the fourth time this week; my mate will really roast me this time.

senses.d: To subject to bantering, severely criticize, sometimes as a comedy routine.
ex: He roasted a bully who then fought with him.

senses.d: To dissipate the volatile parts of by heat, as ores.
